newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Ethnic tension simmers in Indonesia's Kalimantan.
newsitem.headline: Ethnic tension simmers in Indonesia's Kalimantan.

text.p: Ethnic tension still simmered in Indonesia's West Kalimantan province on Friday after renewed clashes between local Dayak tribes and migrants from the island of Madura, residents said on Friday.

They said tension remained high in the provincial capital Pontianak as well as the regional towns of Singkawang and Sanggau. Soldiers have blocked all roads leading to the interior of the province on Borneo Island for the past week.

The tension, which residents say began in late December, exploded on New Year's Day when about 5,000 Dayak tribesman rioted in Sanggau Ledo, 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, attacking the Madurese. At least five died in the clashes.
The attack was set off by a fight over a girl.

Residents in Sanggau, 140 km (87 miles) east of Pontianak, said five Dayaks were killed last week when a crowd of about 200 Dayaks attacked a camp of more than 1,000 Madurese refugees guarded by soldiers.
The Madurese had fled to the town after earlier fighting.
"The soldiers were forced to open fire after they neglected warning shots," one resident said, adding that about 20 people were injured in the incident.
Police in Sanggau acknowledged that clashes had taken place last week but played down the incident and declined to give further details. They said injuries were only light.
"Everybody is now working together," a police sergeant, who declined to be named, told Reuters by telephone from Sanggau.
"The situation is calm and under control," he said, adding a curfew between 9 p.m. and 5 a.m. was still in place in the town.
Officials in other regional towns were not immediately available for comment.
The recent violence prompted Malaysian authorities in the neighbouring state of Sarawak to close the border with West Kalimantan on Sunday in the wake of the ethnic fighting.
Indonesia, the world's most populous Moslem nation, has been rocked by a series of of riots sparked by minor incidents in recent months.

A complaint by an ethnic Chinese woman over noise made by youths calling Moslems to their pre-dawn Ramadan breakfast late last month in a small town east of Jakarta triggered burning of churches and shops.
